title: Wedge Drop
teaches: The Wedge Drop as we use it: a bounce makes a top, stalls a few days on Kell's fast averages, then closes down through them. For every long holder it is the sell signal. It is a short only in the narrow form below the 200-day, in a weak market: short as price trades down through the trigger, never at the close, the stop a few cents over the trigger day's high within about 3%, the first cover is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, the rest on the trail, and a close back above both averages is the exit. We recommend shorting only to traders who have already made $1 million.

facts.quote: The Wedge Drop happens when the market trades back below the moving averages after a strong rally, known as an Exhaustion Extension.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the Wedge Drop is the trade back below the moving averages after a strong rally.

facts.quote: After an Exhaustion Extension, prices often trade in a tight range as moving averages catch up.
facts.claim: TraderLion: after the extension, price trades in a tight range while the averages catch up.

facts.quote: Sometimes, you won’t see a big Exhaustion Extension, but the price will trade sideways and eventually lose momentum.
facts.claim: TraderLion: a Wedge Drop can come without a big extension, out of sideways trade.

facts.quote: If you’re sitting on gains from an earlier entry, use the Wedge Drop as a signal to protect profits and reduce exposure.
facts.claim: TraderLion: for a long holder the Wedge Drop is the signal to protect profits.

facts.quote: As the price breaks below moving averages with increased selling pressure, you can enter a short position with a stop just above the recent high.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the short enters as price breaks below the averages on selling pressure, stop above the recent high.

facts.quote: If the stock regains its moving averages and pushes higher, exit the short position.
facts.claim: TraderLion: if the stock regains its averages, exit the short.

facts.quote: It’s also best to avoid shorting early in new bull markets or strong uptrending stocks.
facts.claim: TraderLion: avoid shorting early in new bull markets or strong uptrending stocks.

facts.quote: So when an index like the S&P 500 or Nasdaq forms a Wedge Drop, it’s a warning that the market as a whole is weakening.
facts.claim: TraderLion: an index Wedge Drop warns that the whole market is weakening.

facts.quote: When several leaders fall below their moving averages in a Wedge Drop pattern, it’s a sign to get defensive.
facts.claim: TraderLion: several leaders in Wedge Drops is a sign to get defensive.

facts.quote: For more aggressive traders, the Wedge Drop can also be an opportunity to go short.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the short is for more aggressive traders.

facts.quote: If you’re more aggressive, shorting can be a good play, but you’ll need to set tight stop-losses and be aware of rising volatility as the stock trends lower.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the short needs tight stops and rising volatility as the stock falls.

facts.quote: Decreased buying volume (accumulation)
facts.claim: TraderLion lists decreased buying volume among the warning signs before the drop.

facts.quote: Increased selling volume (distribution)
facts.claim: TraderLion lists increased selling volume among the warning signs before the drop.

facts.quote: After the Exhaustion Extension, the price will trade tight into the moving averages as there are now fewer new buyers.
facts.claim: Kell's cycle page: after the extension, price trades tight into the averages.

facts.quote: The Wedge Drop confirms the reversal when the price falls through the moving averages with an influx of sellers.
facts.claim: Kell's cycle page: the Wedge Drop is price falling through the averages with an influx of sellers.

facts.quote: 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages guide us through the intermediate-term trend
facts.claim: Kell's pair is the 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages.

facts.quote: Like an EMA Crossback to the upside, an EMA Crossback to the downside will retest the moving averages but is now met with more resistance, pushing the stock lower.
facts.claim: Kell: after the drop, a downside EMA Crossback retests the averages and is met with resistance.

facts.quote: If a stock tops and starts to decline, step aside and let the cycle reset before jumping back in.
facts.claim: Kell's cycle page: once a stock tops, step aside and let the cycle reset.

facts.quote: Hourly and 15-minute charts are for timing entries.
facts.claim: Kell: hourly and 15-minute charts are for timing entries.

facts.quote: Downtrends are volatile, and ideally, any long positions have been closed at the Wedge Drop.

facts.quote: Be careful not to short too late in the downtrend, just like buying late in an uptrend.

facts.claim: A lower-high top peaks under the highest high of the 60 sessions before it.

facts.claim: The stall runs 3 to 10 sessions from the top to the trigger day.

facts.quote: Through the stall no close is more than 1 ATR from the 10-day EMA.
facts.claim: In the stall no close sits more than 1 ATR from the 10-day EMA.

facts.quote: No new high in the last 3 sessions of the stall.
facts.claim: No new high in the stall's last 3 sessions.

facts.quote: In the stall the up days come on lighter volume than the down days.
facts.claim: In the stall the up days are lighter than the down days.

facts.quote: Wide, loose action before the drop is graded down, not excluded.
facts.claim: Wide, loose action before the drop is graded down, not excluded.

facts.quote: The trigger day closes in the lower 40% of its range.
facts.claim: The trigger day closes in the lower 40% of its range.

facts.quote: Advanced: an intraday break of the stall low on the 65-minute chart counts only once the daily close confirms it.

facts.claim: No adding at the crossback; it is a new trade with its own stop.

facts.quote: A close above the trigger day's high: the stop has already gone; the stop is the exit.

questions.q: What happened on the last bar that makes it a Wedge Drop?
choices: A close down through the averages
A close under the 200-day line
A retest of the averages after a drop
A close up through the averages
questions.answer: A close down through the averages
questions.why: A close down through the averages. Kell: the drop confirms the reversal when price falls through the moving averages with an influx of sellers. Before it, price rested tight on them because there were fewer new buyers. So the fall through them shows sellers have taken over. The 200-day is a separate gate for shorts. The chart is META.
questions.lesson_line: A rally, a rest on the averages, then the close through them. That is the drop.

wrong.A close under the 200-day line: The 200-day is the gate for a short. The drop is the close down through the averages the stock rested on.
wrong.A close up through the averages: That is the mirror, the Wedge Pop: a close up through the averages from under them. The drop closes down through them.
wrong.A retest of the averages after a drop: That is the downside EMA Crossback, a retest met with resistance after the drop. The drop is the close down through the averages.

questions.simple: A Wedge Drop is a close down through the moving averages. It shows sellers have taken over from the buyers who held price up.

reasons: fixed before (cold check)

questions.story: The chart ends on the day in question. Compare where the last bar closes with the two fast averages.

questions.q: For us a Wedge Drop above the 200-day is a sell signal for a long, never a short.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our rule is shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short. In our scan a plain Wedge Drop had no edge by itself. It separated from the base rate only for a stock under its 200-day, in a market under its 50-day. Above the 200-day the drop still tells a long holder to sell.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day it tells you to sell. Below it, and only below it, it can be shorted.
questions.simple: True. Our scan found an edge only under the 200-day in a weak market, so above it a Wedge Drop only means sell a long.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, a hard rule)

questions.q: On this chart, what came right before the drop?
choices: An extension, then a tight stall
A base of many months, then a pop
A steady slide with no pause
A gap up out of a flat base
questions.answer: An extension, then a tight stall
questions.why: An extension, then a tight stall. After an Exhaustion Extension, prices often trade in a tight range as moving averages catch up. Kell: price trades tight into the averages because there are fewer new buyers, and then the drop confirms the sellers. A big extension is not always there: sometimes price only trades sideways and loses momentum. The chart is AAPL.
questions.lesson_line: The top, then the rest on the averages, then the drop. Learn the order.

wrong.A base of many months, then a pop: That is a base for a long. The stall before a drop is days, not months.
wrong.A steady slide with no pause: After the extension price rests in a tight range while the averages catch up. The drop follows a rest, not a slide.
wrong.A gap up out of a flat base: That is a breakout. The drop follows a top, not a breakout.

questions.simple: Price stretches out on a rally, then rests tight on its averages because few new buyers are left. The drop comes next.
questions.story: The chart ends on the day price closed under both averages. Look at the days before it.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: No short more than ___% under the trigger level.
questions.why: 4%. We never short more than 4% under the trigger level. It mirrors our no-chase line for longs, 4% past the buy point, because shorts are our long setups reversed. Past 4%, we skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent under the trigger and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.
questions.simple: The limit is 4%. If the price is already more than 4% under the trigger level, we skip the short.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, mirrored by D47)

questions.q: Once a Wedge Drop short is closed out, one new close under both averages is enough for a second short.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A second short needs a new stall and a new close under both averages. The stall is the rest that shows buyers have run out, because there are fewer new buyers (Kell). A failed drop has just shown buyers can take the averages back. One more close under them proves little. Like any re-entry, it is a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
questions.lesson_line: The drop is a one-day event. Once it fails, the next short needs a new setup.
questions.simple: False. A failed drop shows buyers can win back the averages, so a second short needs a new stall first.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a Wedge Drop short, by our default?
choices: A few cents over the trigger day's high
A few cents under the day's low
A few cents over the 200-day line
Exactly on the trigger day's high
questions.answer: A few cents over the trigger day's high
questions.why: A few cents over the trigger day's high. A short loses when price rises, so the stop goes above the entry. The high of the day that confirmed the drop is the nearest place the idea is wrong. A stop there keeps the loss small. It sits a few cents past the high, not on it. We want a clear invalidation spot. We prefer stops 1 to 3% away and accept up to 5%. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents over the trigger day's high, not exactly on it.

wrong.A few cents under the day's low: That is the long's stop, mirrored the wrong way. A short's risk is above the entry.
wrong.A few cents over the 200-day line: The 200-day is the gate for taking the short, not the place for its stop. The stop goes over the trigger day's high.
wrong.Exactly on the trigger day's high: Our rule is a few cents past the day's extreme, not exactly on it.

questions.simple: A short loses when price rises, so the stop sits a few cents over the trigger day's high, where the idea fails.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-008, where the stop goes)

questions.story: The chart ends on the trigger day, the day you short.

questions.q: On our card the stall runs 3 to 10 sessions between the top and the trigger day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The card says the stall runs 3 to 10 sessions between the top and the trigger day. Those numbers are the card's, not Kell's. He only says that after the extension, price trades tight into the moving averages as there are fewer new buyers.
questions.lesson_line: Three to ten days of rest on the averages. Then the close decides.
questions.simple: True. Our card gives the stall three to ten sessions between the top and the trigger day.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number

questions.q: What is that a warning of?
choices: The whole market is weakening
Only a few big stocks are tired
A pause before the next leg up
A buy point for the market leaders
questions.answer: The whole market is weakening
questions.why: The market as a whole is weakening. TraderLion: when an index like the S&P 500 or Nasdaq forms a Wedge Drop, it is a warning. Several leaders in Wedge Drops is a sign to get defensive. Bracco read the Nasdaq's drop as the start of another leg down. The chart is QQQ in a bear market: a bounce made a lower high and then dropped, and the lows over the next weeks sat well under the trigger close.
questions.lesson_line: An index Wedge Drop is a warning for the whole market, not just one stock.

wrong.A buy point for the market leaders: Several leaders in Wedge Drops is a sign to get defensive, not to buy.
wrong.Only a few big stocks are tired: TraderLion: an index Wedge Drop warns that the market as a whole is weakening, not a few names.
wrong.A pause before the next leg up: Bracco read the Nasdaq's drop as the start of another leg down. Kell read an index drop as confirmation of a deeper pullback.

questions.simple: A Wedge Drop in the index warns that the whole market is getting weaker, not just one stock.

deeper.example: Kell dated this on QQQ: an Exhaustion Extension on 2/2, a Wedge Drop on 2/16 and 2/17, an EMA Crossback on 2/23. That index drop sat above the 200-day, so for us it was a sell signal for longs, not a short.

reasons: a card rule, proposed

questions.story: Hidden index fund, the trigger day is the last bar. The index itself forms a Wedge Drop.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A short still under 1R of profit after ___ sessions is covered.
questions.why: 10. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is closed, which frees the money. For a short, closed means covered.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: After 10 trading days with less than 1R of profit, we cover the short and free the money for something better.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, the time stop)

questions.q: Before the trigger day, how many of the last 10 closes must sit above the 20-day EMA on our card?
choices: At least 5
At least 7
At least 8
At least 9
questions.answer: At least 8
questions.why: At least 8 of the 10. The card wants at least 8 of the 10 closes before the trigger day above the 20-day EMA. That is the prior bounce. For a short, Kell drew it as a fast rally in a bear market. It puts in a lower high and then drops. A dip under the 20-day is allowed, so it does not need all 10. The 8 is the card's proposed number.
questions.lesson_line: No bounce, no drop. Eight of the last ten closes over the 20-day EMA is the bounce.

wrong.At least 5: Five of ten is only half the closes. The card wants eight.
wrong.At least 7: Seven of ten falls short. The card wants eight.
wrong.At least 9: Nine is stricter than the card. A dip under the 20-day is allowed, and eight of ten is the line.

questions.simple: At least 8 of the last 10 closes must sit above the 20-day average. That is what makes it a bounce.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number
tied to a held decision (D-021)

questions.story: The stock has an RS rating of 92 and leads its group. It stalls four days on its averages, then closes under them, under the 200-day.
questions.q: Short it?
choices: No; a leader, not the weakest
Yes; it closed under the averages
Yes; RS does not matter on shorts
questions.answer: No; a leader, not the weakest
questions.why: No. Shorts are the mirror: the weakest stocks, an RS rating of 20 or less, in the weakest groups. A leader with strong RS is the B- row, and TraderLion says to avoid strong uptrending stocks.
questions.lesson_line: Short the weakest, not the strongest. A leader that lost its averages once is not weak.

wrong.Yes; it closed under the averages: The close is one gate. The RS rule is another, and a 92 fails it.
wrong.Yes; RS does not matter on shorts: It matters in mirror image: 20 or less, in a weak group.

questions.q: A Wedge Drop short in a $6 stock trading $3 million a day is fine if the chart is clean.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one is $6 and $3 million, so it fails both. A trader needs a stock that trades enough to get in and out. A thin one can jump on small orders and be hard to cover, and a clean chart does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: Price and liquidity come before the chart. Under $10 or under $20 million a day, pass.
questions.simple: False. A stock this thin is hard to get out of, and we trade only $10 stocks with $20 million a day.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: You hold a long and did not sell the second extension. By Kell's deck, what takes you out?
choices: The Wedge Drop signal
The EMA Crossback retest
The Wedge Pop breakout
A close under the 200-day
questions.answer: The Wedge Drop signal
questions.why: The Wedge Drop. Kell: if you did not sell the second extension, let the Wedge Drop protect you and take you out of the trade. TraderLion agrees: use it as a signal to protect profits and reduce exposure. Holding a long through a real drop gives the gains back. If it was only a shakeout, we buy again on a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: The drop is the last exit for a long. Not a reason to hope.

wrong.The EMA Crossback retest: The crossback comes after the drop. Kell: ideally any long positions have been closed at the Wedge Drop.
wrong.The Wedge Pop breakout: A pop is a close up through the averages, the mirror setup. It is a buy setup, not an exit.
wrong.A close under the 200-day: Kell names the drop as the backstop. The 200-day is where longs stop being allowed, not his exit signal.

questions.simple: The Wedge Drop. It protects the gains you made, and if it was a shakeout we simply buy again on a new setup.

questions.q: No new Wedge Drop short in the 3 sessions before an earnings report.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We take no new trades in the 3 days before a report, and the same goes for a short. A report can gap the stock past your stop overnight, and a tight stop cannot catch a gap. A short you already hold stays through a report only if it is up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: No new short in the 3 sessions before a report.
questions.simple: True. A report can gap the stock past your stop overnight, so we open no new short in the 3 days before it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: In the stall, how far may a close sit from the 9 EMA on our card?
choices: No more than 0.5 ATR
No more than 1 ATR
No more than 2 ATR
No more than 5%
questions.answer: No more than 1 ATR
questions.why: No more than 1 ATR. Through the stall no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. ATR is the stock's own usual daily range, so the test fits each stock. Kell: price trades tight into the moving averages. The 1 ATR is the card's proposed number.
questions.lesson_line: The stall hugs the 9 EMA. Far from it is not a stall.

wrong.No more than 5%: The stall test is set in ATR, the stock's own usual daily range, not in a fixed percent.
wrong.No more than 0.5 ATR: That is stricter than the card. The line is 1 ATR.
wrong.No more than 2 ATR: Too loose. The card's line is 1 ATR from the 9 EMA.

questions.simple: No close in the stall sits more than one typical day's range away from the 9 EMA.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number
tied to a held decision (D-021)

questions.story: In a bear market the stock bounces into its falling 50-day, turns down under its earlier high, then stalls four days. The chart ends the day before the drop.
questions.q: What kind of top is that?
choices: A lower high, the bear-market form
An extension top over the 20-day
A failed push past the prior day's high
No top yet; it is only a pause
questions.answer: A lower high, the bear-market form
questions.why: A lower high. The bounce peaked under the earlier high and was turned back at a falling average. We want shorts on a decent pop back up that is rejected at the 50-day or 20-day, below the 200-day. Kell's bear-market diagram is the same: a fast rally puts in a lower high, then drops. A rally that cannot clear its old high shows buyers are weakening, and a stop just over the top is close.
questions.lesson_line: A pop into the falling 50-day that fails is the picture we want.

wrong.An extension top over the 20-day: An extension is a close far above the 20-day EMA. This bounce died at a falling average.
wrong.A failed push past the prior day's high: That is one day failing to clear the prior day's high. This bounce peaked well under the earlier high.
wrong.No top yet; it is only a pause: A bounce that turns under the prior high and stalls is the top. The drop then confirms it.

questions.simple: The bounce peaked under the earlier high and was rejected at a falling average, which shows buyers are weakening.

deeper.example: WHR in a bear market was this picture. A bear-market bounce made a lower high at the falling 50-day, a four-day stall followed, and the close under both averages came the next day. The averages then led it down.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: A close under both averages, after a bounce still making new highs, is already a Wedge Drop.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A stall is a rest on the averages, and a bounce still making new highs has not rested. Kell: price trades tight into the averages because there are fewer new buyers. New highs mean buyers are still in charge. Shorting a leader at its highs is a named mistake, and the stop over the high is taken at once. Wait for quiet days and a fresh stall.
questions.lesson_line: A stall that keeps making highs is not stalling. Wait for the quiet days.
questions.simple: False. While price still makes new highs, buyers are in charge, so there is no stall yet and no drop to short.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The trigger day gaps down and opens 12% under its 9 EMA. The stall and the averages all checked out.
questions.q: Short at the open, or pass?
choices: Pass; over 10% under the 9 EMA
Pass; the stall was too short
Short; gap confirms the top
Short at half size, same stop
questions.answer: Pass; over 10% under the 9 EMA
questions.why: Pass. We skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA, and the short is the same rule reversed. This one opens 12% under, so most of the quick move is done and a short here is a chase. It is our too-stretched rule for longs, reversed.
questions.lesson_line: A drop that is already stretched is a chase with a different name.

wrong.Pass; the stall was too short: The story says the stall checked out. The reason to pass is the stretch under the 9 EMA.
wrong.Short; gap confirms the top: A gap down can look like confirmation. The stretch rule still says skip.
wrong.Short at half size, same stop: Size does not fix a stretched entry. The rule is skip.

At exactly 3R, whatever the day
Never; hold it all to the end

wrong.At exactly 3R, whatever the day: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.

Hold; your stop is still above it
Add; it is now a better price
Move the stop to breakeven

wrong.Add; it is now a better price: Full size at one price with one stop. A reclaimed drop is a cancelled setup, not a second entry.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell, once the trade has paid. A reclaim says cover.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.

questions.simple: Two R is 44.10, the fill minus twice the stop distance. Moving the stop to breakeven there means the trade cannot become a loser.

Buy the dip; the market is Green
Short; the stock is under its 200
Short, but at half size only

Yes; any close under both averages works
Yes, if volume was heavy that day
No; it must close at the day's low

wrong.No; it must close at the day's low: The card asks for the lower 40% of the range, not the exact low. A close near the low counts.

Up days heavier than down days
Up and down days on equal volume
Volume rising on every day

questions.lesson_line: Quiet up days, heavier down days. Fewer new buyers while price rests on the averages.

wrong.Up days heavier than down days: That is buyers stepping in, not fading. The card wants the up days lighter.
wrong.Up and down days on equal volume: The card wants the up days lighter than the down days, not equal.
wrong.Volume rising on every day: The stall wants quiet up days. Rising volume every day is not a rest.

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
choices: 37.55, the first 30-minute high
37.05, the first 30-minute low
37.40, the price at the open
Cover; the gap is past 2R
questions.answer: 37.55, the first 30-minute high
questions.why: 37.55. A stop cannot catch an overnight gap, so the old stop at 37.22 is already gone. The first 30 minutes show where price settles. For a short, the high of that first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. This is the one time a stop may move wider. If the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you get out. Here they have not.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Cover; the gap is past 2R: The ceiling is 2R. The loss at the 37.55 high is still under it, so it has not been hit.
wrong.37.05, the first 30-minute low: That is the long's rule, mirrored the wrong way. A short's risk is above, so the high is the stop.
wrong.37.40, the price at the open: The gap rule gives the decision to the first 30 minutes. The open is not the stop.

questions.q: At the rally back into the falling averages you may add to the short, since Kell's page says so.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Kell's page does offer the EMA Crossback as a place to add to a short started at the Wedge Drop. Our rule is full size at one price with one stop. We pick the size from the stop before we enter. An add after the stock has moved makes the position bigger than that plan, so the loss at the stop grows. The crossback can only be its own new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop. The crossback is a new trade or nothing.
questions.simple: False. Adding makes the position bigger than the stop allowed, so we take full size once, with one stop.

deeper.counter: Kell says the crossback gives a clear area to set a stop against. We take that as the stop for a new trade, sized from that stop. It is not a place to add to the old one.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, over a web view)

questions.story: Mid-morning the stock trades down through both averages and through its stall low. The stall checked out.
questions.q: How do you enter?
choices: Short at market as it trades through
A limit order well above the market
Wait for the close, then short
Short in the after-hours session
questions.answer: Short at market as it trades through
questions.why: Short at market as it trades through the trigger. Every setup, long or short, enters as price trades through its trigger during the day, never at the close. Our entries are market orders, and we take no new entries outside regular hours. Waiting for the close lets the stock run away from the trigger. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays over the high, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Short as price trades through the trigger. Never wait for the close, never enter after hours.

wrong.Short in the after-hours session: We take no new entries outside regular trading hours.
wrong.A limit order well above the market: A limit above the market may never fill on the day that matters. Our entries are market orders.
wrong.Wait for the close, then short: Every setup enters as price trades through its trigger, never at the close. Waiting lets the stock run away from the trigger.

questions.simple: Short at market as price trades through the trigger. Waiting for the close lets the stock run away and costs size.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 and E58)

questions.story: A clean five-day stall breaks under both averages on Monday. The company reports after the close on Tuesday.
questions.q: Short it?
choices: No; a report inside 3 sessions
No; the stall is too short
Yes, at half the usual size
Yes, but cover before the report
questions.answer: No; a report inside 3 sessions
questions.why: No. We take no new short in the 3 sessions before a report. A Monday trigger with a report after Tuesday's close falls inside that window. A report can gap the stock past your stop overnight, and a stop cannot catch a gap. Wait for the report to pass, then look for a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A report inside 3 sessions is a no. Let it pass, then look for a new trigger.

wrong.No; the stall is too short: Five days of rest is fine for a stall. The reason to pass is the report.
wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Size does not fix a report risk. Smaller is still in.
wrong.Yes, but cover before the report: The rule bars the new entry itself in the 3 sessions before a report. Planning to cover early does not change that.

questions.simple: No. A report can gap the stock past your stop, so we open no new short that close to earnings.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, 3 days against 3 sessions)

questions.q: When does the stop move to breakeven on a Wedge Drop short?
choices: From 2R to 5R, or at the first sell
The day after entry, to be safe
Never; a short's stop stays where set
At 1R, once it has paid a bit
questions.answer: From 2R to 5R, or at the first sell
questions.why: From 2R to 5R, or at the first sell, as a judgment. Breakeven is the point after which a trade can no longer turn into a loser. A stop may move in your favour, never wider. Move it too early and ordinary swings can stop you out of a trade that was working.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. A judgment, not a fixed day.

wrong.The day after entry, to be safe: Too early. The trade has not paid yet, and ordinary swings would stop you out. Our window starts at 2R.
wrong.Never; a short's stop stays where set: A stop may move in your favour. Only a wider stop is banned.
wrong.At 1R, once it has paid a bit: Too early. Our window starts at 2R.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. By then the trade has paid, so it should never turn into a loser.

reasons: the breakeven range comes from the card

questions.story: Three weeks after a market low the index is still weak. A stock bounces, stalls three days and closes under both averages at 52.58.
questions.q: What risk does our card name here?
choices: Early in a new bull market
The stall is too long for a drop
The stop is too far
The volume is too light
questions.answer: Early in a new bull market
questions.why: Early in a new bull market. Our card says no short early in a new bull market, in a strongly uptrending stock, or too late in the fall. TraderLion warns the same way. In the real GOOGL case on 2019-01-14, three weeks after the December 2018 low, the short was stopped the next session at 0R. The stock was 7.2% above the entry 20 sessions later.
questions.lesson_line: A few weeks off a market low, the bounce is the trend. Do not short it.

wrong.The stall is too long for a drop: Three days is inside the 3 to 10 the card allows.
wrong.The stop is too far: GOOGL's stop was 2.1% away, inside 3%. The distance was fine; the timing was not.
wrong.The volume is too light: Volume grades the day. The risk the card names is the new bull market.

questions.simple: The card warns against shorting early in a new bull market, because the bounce can keep going.

deeper.trap: The index still looked weak: QQQ was under its 50-day on GOOGL's trigger day. But it was only three weeks after the December 2018 low. A weak-looking market does not make it safe to short early in a new bull market.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed criteria and dated example numbers

questions.q: If the honest stop over the trigger day's high is 5% away, you pull it in to 3% to fit.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. If the stop over the trigger day's high is more than about 3% away, you skip the trade or take the smaller size the rules give. You never pull it in. Stop first. The size comes from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.
questions.simple: False. If the honest stop is more than about 3% away, we skip the trade or size down, and we never pull the stop in.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A13)

questions.story: Your short sits at 2.7R at Thursday's close. Friday it gaps down and opens at 3.5R.
questions.q: What do you do about the first cover?

Cover a third at the open
Cover the whole position now
Add more; the gap confirms it
questions.answer: Judge it; 3R is not a cover order
questions.why: Judge it. The first cover is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. Selling part into a big gap is an optional choice, never a rule. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. We sell into strength, and a gap is strength, so selling some can be fair. A fixed order would cut a winner that keeps running. A gap in your favour is not a place to add.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R is not a cover order. Judge the first cover.

wrong.Add more; the gap confirms it: Full size at one price. A gap in your favour is not a place to add.
wrong.Cover the whole position now: Nothing says a gap means covering it all. The first cover is a judgment.
wrong.Cover a third at the open: The first cover is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (the first sell is a judgment)
the short side mirrors the long side (D47)

questions.story: The chart ends on the trigger day. An 8-day stall 9.6% wide breaks under both averages. The stop over the day's high is 2.4% away. Our grade is our judgment of how clean a setup is, and it sets the size.
questions.q: How does a wide, loose stall like that change the trade?
choices: It grades lower, and the size follows
It cancels the trade; wide is a no
Full grade; a 2.4% stop is tight
It raises the grade; more room to fall
questions.answer: It grades lower, and the size follows
questions.why: It grades lower, and the size follows the grade. Kell: price rests tight on the averages because there are fewer new buyers. A wide, loose stall is a messier rest than that, so the setup is less clean. We grade by judgment, and the grade sets the size, so a messier setup tends to get less. It is not a no-trade, and a tight stop does not repair it. DXCM in April 2022 had this stall, and the short was stopped at 0R by one more push up.

wrong.It raises the grade; more room to fall: Loose action is less clean, not better. More room to fall is not a grade.

A healthy trend; nothing to do yet
A Wedge Drop, already confirmed

Equal; only averages matter
Drop A; more room to fall

184 shares
140 shares
1,404 shares

Still short; the stop needs a close
Covered at the close, 54.33
Stopped; you may re-short at once

questions.story: The chart is an index fund with its name hidden. A Wedge Drop happened a few days earlier. The chart ends on the day price rallied back to the falling averages and stalled under them.

A Wedge Pop, a buy signal
A reclaim; the drop has failed
questions.answer: A crossback, a retest of the averages
questions.why: A crossback. Kell: a downside EMA Crossback retests the moving averages but is now met with more resistance, pushing the stock lower. His own QQQ sequence ran an extension, then the Wedge Drop, then the EMA Crossback. If you are short, a rally that stalls under the falling averages is a place to hold. The trail still covers on a close back above them. It is not a place to add: that would be a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: The first rally into the falling averages is expected. Hold it, and let the trail speak.

wrong.A new Wedge Drop, a second short: A second drop needs a new stall and a new close under both. This is a rally back up to the averages.
wrong.A Wedge Pop, a buy signal: A pop closes up through both averages out of a coil. This rally stalled under them.
wrong.A reclaim; the drop has failed: Failed means a close back above both averages. This rally stalled under them.

questions.simple: It is a downside crossback, a retest that meets resistance at the falling averages, so a short holds and does not add.

deeper.trap: A crossback is not a failure. The setup fails on a close back above both averages. Adding at the crossback is the common slip, and Kell's own page offers it. Our rule says no: one price and one stop, and a crossback is a new trade or nothing.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
tied to a held decision (D-002)

questions.q: The chart grades A+, our cleanest. But the stock is hard to borrow, with a high fee. Your call?
choices: Skip it; the borrow comes first
Skip it; chart is stretched
Short it at half size
Short it; the A+ chart wins
questions.answer: Skip it; the borrow comes first
questions.why: Skip it. We skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow or the borrow fee is high, however good the chart is. You pay the fee for every day you stay short. A hard-to-borrow stock may not be there to short or to keep. Half size does not help, because the stock fails the rule before size comes up.
questions.lesson_line: A short you cannot borrow cleanly is not a short. Skip it.

wrong.Skip it; chart is stretched: The chart is an A+ Wedge Drop, so it is not the problem. The reason to skip is the borrow.
wrong.Short it at half size: Half of a hard borrow is still a hard borrow. The rule is skip.
wrong.Short it; the A+ chart wins: The borrow comes before the chart. A+ is our judgment of how clean the chart is, and it cannot fix a hard borrow.

questions.simple: Skip it. A hard-to-borrow stock costs a fee every day and may not stay available, so the chart cannot save it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D48)

questions.q: A blow-off top shorted on its climax day above the 200-day is the Parabolic Short's trade, not a Wedge Drop.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A short above the 200-day after a blow-off is the Parabolic Short, taken on its climax day with its own checklist. The Wedge Drop comes days later, after a stall within 1 ATR of the 10-day EMA. Bracco's target for the Parabolic Short is the 9-day EMA, which acts as a magnet for mean reversion.
questions.lesson_line: Shorting the blow-off is a different setup. The Wedge Drop comes days later, back at the averages.
questions.simple: True. Shorting a blow-off on its climax day is the Parabolic Short, and a Wedge Drop comes days later.

deeper.counter: Timing separates the two. A Parabolic Short is the climax day of a 3 to 5 day burst, 10% or more over the 9-day EMA. A Wedge Drop needs the stall first, then the close through the averages.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-040, the parabolic exception)

questions.story: A stock in an uptrend bounces, stalls on its averages and closes under both. The close is 8.3% above its 200-day.
questions.q: What is it for us?
choices: A sell signal for a long, not a short
An A+ short
A Wedge Pop
A parabolic short
questions.answer: A sell signal for a long, not a short
questions.why: A sell signal, not a short. Shorts only below the 200-day. V 2021-05-10 was this, above the 200-day in an uptrend. The short ran 0.93R and was stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day the drop tells a long holder to sell. It gives a short seller nothing.

wrong.An A+ short: No short above the 200-day, however clean the stall. That is a hard rule.
wrong.A Wedge Pop: A pop closes up through the averages. This closed down through them.
wrong.A parabolic short: A parabolic short is a climax day after a 3 to 5 day burst. This is a stall and a drop.

questions.story: The trigger day is the last bar. In the stall, one close sits more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. Then the stock closes under both averages.
questions.q: Does that pass our stall test?
choices: No; one close was past 1 ATR
Yes; the stall was long enough
Yes; that distance is fine
No; the stall was too short
questions.answer: No; one close was past 1 ATR
questions.why: No. Through the stall no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. One close past 1 ATR fails that test. The stall's length is inside the 3 to 10 the card allows, so length is not the problem. The 1 ATR is the card's proposed number. WFC was this near miss: an extension turn with no real stall, the mean-reversion short and not a Wedge Drop.
questions.lesson_line: Count the quiet days. One close too far from the 9 EMA and it is not a stall.

wrong.Yes; the stall was long enough: Length is one test. The distance is another, and one close failed it.
wrong.No; the stall was too short: The stall's length is inside the 3 to 10 sessions the card allows. The distance is what fails.
wrong.Yes; that distance is fine: The card says no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. This one is past it.

questions.simple: No. One close past 1 ATR from the 9 EMA breaks the stall test, even when the stall is long enough.

deeper.trap: One stretched close breaks a stall. A close that far from the 9 EMA means the move is still extended with no real stall, so it is not a Wedge Drop.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The trigger day is the last bar. In the stall the up days averaged 2.84 times the volume of the down days. Then a close under both averages.
questions.q: What was the stall?
choices: Accumulation; buyers had not run out
A clean stall; the up days were quiet
Distribution; sellers were in charge
Exhaustion; the buyers were all spent
questions.answer: Accumulation; buyers had not run out
questions.why: Accumulation; buyers had not run out. In a clean stall the volume dries up on the up days, because there are fewer new buyers. Here the up days ran 2.84 times the volume of the down days. So buyers were stepping in and the rest was not over, which makes this a weak short. VZ in June 2010 did this, and the short was stopped as the stock rallied through the averages.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy up days in the stall mean someone is buying. That is a weak short.

wrong.A clean stall; the up days were quiet: The story says the up days ran 2.84 times the volume of the down days. That is not quiet, and volume dries up in a clean stall.
wrong.Distribution; sellers were in charge: Heavy up days mean buyers, not sellers. Distribution is the reverse: heavier selling volume.
wrong.Exhaustion; the buyers were all spent: Heavy volume on the up days means buyers were still stepping in. Spent buyers would show quiet up days.

questions.simple: Heavy volume on the up days means buyers were stepping in, so the rest was not over and the short is weak.

deeper.trap: The close under both averages is only one gate. The stall's volume is another, and here it failed. VZ looked like a Wedge Drop on the chart, ran 0.54R, then was stopped as the stock rallied through the averages.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The stock is 25% over its 9 EMA on the fifth straight up day. It gaps up, then closes red.
questions.q: Which setup is that?
choices: The Parabolic Short, climax day
A Wedge Drop, after a quiet stall
A Wedge Pop, out of a tight coil
A downside crossback, a retest
questions.answer: The Parabolic Short, climax day
questions.why: The Parabolic Short. It is shorted on the climax day of a burst of up days, with price far above its 9 EMA. Here the stock is 25% over it on the fifth straight up day. A Wedge Drop comes days later, after price has rested on its averages. Bracco's target for a parabolic short is the 9-day EMA, which acts as a magnet for mean reversion. The two setups have different plans, so name the setup before you plan the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the distance to the averages. Far above them on the climax day is the other setup.

wrong.A Wedge Drop, after a quiet stall: No stall on the averages, and price is far above them. The drop comes days later, back at the averages.
wrong.A Wedge Pop, out of a tight coil: A pop is a close up through the averages out of a coil. This is a blow-off far above them.
wrong.A downside crossback, a retest: A crossback is a rally back into the averages after a drop. Nothing has dropped yet.

questions.simple: Far above its 9 EMA on a climax day is a Parabolic Short. Its target is the 9 EMA, which acts as a magnet.

deeper.trap: Distance is the tell. A Wedge Drop stalls on its averages. A Parabolic Short sits far above its 9 EMA after a burst of up days. The same red close can show up in both, one at the averages and the other far above them.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
tied to a held decision (D-040)

questions.story: Price just closed through both EMAs. For two weeks before today it had coiled under them. Today it closed up through both.
questions.q: Which is it?
choices: A Wedge Pop, the mirror setup
A Wedge Drop, a sell signal
A downside crossback, a test
An upside crossback, a test
questions.answer: A Wedge Pop, the mirror setup
questions.why: A Wedge Pop. Look at where price sat before the day and which way it closed. A Wedge Pop coils under the two fast averages and closes up through both. A Wedge Drop rests on or just above them and closes down through both. Kell: many traders wrongly think the pop is simply a cross of the averages. Price bars and volume matter too, so where price rested is what tells the two apart.
questions.lesson_line: Same averages, opposite sides. Which side it came from and which way it closed is the whole tell.

wrong.A Wedge Drop, a sell signal: A drop closes down through the averages from on or just above them. This closed up through them from below.
wrong.A downside crossback, a test: A downside crossback is a rally that stalls under falling averages and is met with resistance. This closed up through them.
wrong.An upside crossback, a test: A crossback is a retest of the averages. This is the first close up through both.

questions.simple: Price coiled under both averages and then closed up through them, so it is a Wedge Pop. Where price rested tells them apart.

deeper.trap: A close through the averages is not enough to name the setup. Which side price came from decides it. Coiled under and closed up through both is the Pop. Stalled on or above and closed down through both is the Drop. Kell also warns the pop is not simply a cross, since price bars and volume matter.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-078)

questions.q: An intraday break of the stall low on the 65-minute chart counts only once the daily close confirms it.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Kell says hourly and 15-minute charts are for timing entries. Our card counts a break of the stall low on the 65-minute chart only once the daily close confirms it. The daily close is the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: The hourly chart can sharpen the entry. The daily close is still the judge.
questions.simple: True. The hourly break can help time the entry, but our card counts it only after the daily close confirms it.

deeper.trap: Shorting inside the stall before the close confirms is a named mistake. An intraday break of the stall low is only a hint until the daily close confirms it. The drop is a one-day event that the next day confirms or cancels.

reasons: rests on a proposed advanced card rule

questions.q: The 9 EMA is 40.00 and the stock opens at 36.40. How far under the average is the open, in percent?
questions.why: 9.0%. The open is under the average by (40.00 - 36.40) / 40.00 x 100 = 9.0%. That is under 10%, so this test does not stop the short at that open. We skip a short more than 10% under its 9 EMA, checked at the open on a gap down.
questions.lesson_line: Check the stretch at the open on a gap down. Past 10% under the 9 EMA, pass.
questions.simple: Take the average minus the open and divide by the average. That is 9.0%, under the 10% line, so this test lets the short through.

deeper.trap: Divide by the average, not by the open. The average is the line the open sits under. Use average minus open, over average.

reasons: +2 a computed key

wrong.9.9%: Divided by the open, not by the average.
wrong.3.6%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.0.9%: A decimal slip. The open is far more than one percent under the average.

questions.story: A failed-push top, a three-day stall, a drop on 3.3x volume. You shorted at 24.74, stop 25.26. It never passes 0.34R; on day 8 the stop is hit.
questions.q: Was that loss a mistake?
choices: No; a planned loss, the stop worked
No; you should have covered at 0.34R
Yes; 3.3x volume said stay out
Yes; the stop was far too tight
questions.answer: No; a planned loss, the stop worked
questions.why: No. A stop hit is the plan working. The stop is the exit and is never widened. This one sat 2.1% over the 24.74 fill, inside the 3% a stop usually stays within. The trade peaked at 0.34R and was stopped on day 8. Volume on the drop does not change what a stop-out is.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working. You will take this one again.

wrong.Yes; the stop was far too tight: It sat 2.1% over the fill, inside the usual 3%, and it held until day 8.
wrong.No; you should have covered at 0.34R: Nothing in the plan covers at 0.34R. The first cover is a third at 3R, and the stop is the exit.
wrong.Yes; 3.3x volume said stay out: Volume on the drop grades the day. It does not make a stop-out at plan a mistake.

questions.simple: No. A stop hit is the plan working, because the stop is the exit and the loss was the one we planned.

deeper.trap: A loss is not a mistake just because the setup failed. Judge the trade against the plan: stop first, stop respected, never widened. This trade reached only 0.34R before the stop. That is how a stop works, not a breach of the plan.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-006, trigger volume)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: You held a long. It closed under both averages and you sold. Two sessions later it closes back above both and runs.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Nothing; buy only on a new setup
Buy back now; it was a shakeout
Short it; it will fail again
Wait a few days, then buy it back
questions.answer: Nothing; buy only on a new setup
questions.why: Nothing yet. A Wedge Drop reclaimed within a few sessions was a shakeout. Selling was still right, because the drop is the last exit for a long. In our scan, 38.2% of drops closed back above both averages within 3 sessions, so some shakeouts are normal. Kell: once a stock tops, step aside and let the cycle reset before jumping back in. Buy again only on a new setup, as a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout is not a buy signal. The next setup is.

wrong.Buy back now; it was a shakeout: Knowing it was a shakeout is not a trigger. The re-entry needs its own setup and its own stop.
wrong.Short it; it will fail again: It just reclaimed both averages. Shorting a reclaim is fighting strength with no setup.
wrong.Wait a few days, then buy it back: A clock is not a trigger. Buy again only when the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop.

questions.simple: Do nothing yet. Selling was right, and we buy again only when a new setup triggers, with its own stop.

deeper.trap: The hindsight trap is feeling that selling was a mistake because it reclaimed and ran. The rule did not change. Selling at the drop was the plan, and getting back in is a new decision with a new stop. Shorting the reclaim is the opposite error, fighting a stock that just took back both averages.

reasons: a card rule built on the settled re-entry rule

questions.story: The trigger day is the last bar. The stall breaks on a gap down and every other rule checks out. The fill is 90.85 and the stop over the high is 93.53, 3.0% away.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: Yes; 3.0% is a fair stop distance
No; never short a gap down
Yes, but pull the stop to 2%
No; any stop past 2% is a pass
questions.answer: Yes; 3.0% is a fair stop distance
questions.why: Yes. We prefer stops 1 to 3% away, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% is acceptable, so 3.0% is fine. The stop sets the size: with the same risk, a wider stop buys fewer shares. Never pull the stop in to fit, because it then sits inside the day's range, where one more push up takes it. TSM on 2022-06-09 was this trade: it opened under the prior low and closed under the stall low. It reached 6.4R at best, with 3R on day 9.
questions.lesson_line: A 3% stop is fine. Up to 5% is acceptable, and never pull a stop in to fit.

wrong.No; never short a gap down: A gap down closing near its low is a fine trigger day. The question is only the stop's distance.
wrong.Yes, but pull the stop to 2%: Never pull the stop in to fit. It sits over the high or the trade is skipped.
wrong.No; any stop past 2% is a pass: Our preferred stop is 1 to 3% and up to 5% is acceptable, so 3.0% is not a pass.

questions.simple: Take it. 3.0% is inside the 5% we accept, and the stop sets the size, so a wider stop just means fewer shares.

deeper.trap: The trap is the fix. If the stop were past 5%, we would mostly wait for a tighter trigger. We never pull the stop in to make it fit. Here nothing needs fixing: 3.0% is inside the 1 to 3% we prefer.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.story: Ten sessions after the short, the trade is up 1.4R and drifting sideways on the averages.
questions.q: What does our rule say?
choices: Hold; it is past the 1R bar
Cover; ten sessions is the limit
Cover; it has stopped moving
Add on a pop to the averages
questions.answer: Hold; it is past the 1R bar
questions.why: Hold. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days, freeing the money for something better. This one is up 1.4R, so it has done something and the time stop does not apply. The stop, the covers and the trail still run the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after ten days, out. Past 1R, the other rules run the trade.

wrong.Cover; ten sessions is the limit: The time stop covers a trade still under 1R after 10 sessions. This one is past 1R.
wrong.Cover; it has stopped moving: Drifting alone is not the rule. Under 1R after 10 sessions is.
wrong.Add on a pop to the averages: No adding. Full size at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Hold. The time stop frees money from trades that have done nothing, and this one is up 1.4R.

deeper.trap: Reading the rule as 'ten days and out' is the slip. The bar is 1R of profit, and 1.4R clears it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.story: The company reported last night. Today, after a six-day stall on the averages, it gaps down and closes under both, near its low.
questions.q: Does the earnings rule block this short?
choices: No; the reaction day is allowed
Yes; no shorts near earnings
Yes; wait 3 sessions post-report
No; earnings only blocks longs
questions.answer: No; the reaction day is allowed
questions.why: No. The rule is no new short in the 3 sessions before a report. The reason is the overnight gap, which a stop cannot catch. Once the report is out that risk is over, so a Wedge Drop that is the earnings reaction itself is allowed. The report here came last night, so the sessions before it are over.
questions.lesson_line: Before the report, wait. The reaction day can be the drop.

wrong.Yes; no shorts near earnings: The rule bars new shorts in the 3 sessions before a report. This report is already out.
wrong.Yes; wait 3 sessions post-report: There is no waiting period after a report. The gap through the averages is the trigger.
wrong.No; earnings only blocks longs: The 3-session rule covers new shorts too. It is the report being over that frees this one.

questions.simple: No. The rule guards against the gap before a report, and this report is already out.

deeper.trap: There are two ways to get this wrong. One is shorting in the 3 sessions before the report, which the rule bars. The other is treating the reaction day as blocked too. The rule counts the 3 sessions before a report, not the days after it. The other gates still apply, so the drop still needs its stall and its close under both averages.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: By our rules, which RS rating fits a Wedge Drop short?
choices: 20 or less, in a weak group
80 or more, strong group
Any rating; chart decides
50 or less, weak group
questions.answer: 20 or less, in a weak group
questions.why: 20 or less, in a weak group. Shorts are the mirror of buying leaders: the weakest stocks, an RS rating of 20 or less, in the weakest groups. An RS rating of 20 or less means the stock lags the market. Shorting a leader at its highs is a named mistake, because strong stocks keep going and the stop is taken. In our own words, we are extremely picky with shorts.
questions.lesson_line: Short the weakest in the weakest groups. The mirror of buying leaders.

wrong.80 or more, strong group: That is the leader's side. Shorts are the mirror: the weakest stocks in the weakest groups.
wrong.Any rating; chart decides: The chart is one gate. Weakness is another.
wrong.50 or less, weak group: The line is 20 or less, not 50.

questions.simple: Shorts mirror buying leaders: the weakest stocks in the weakest groups, because strong stocks keep going and take the stop.

deeper.trap: RS of 20 or less is a gate, not a trigger. The stock also needs the 200-day, the market reading, the stall and the close through the averages. We are extremely picky: one or two shorts per cycle.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C31, the short mirror)

questions.story: The trigger level was 64.63. You were away from the screen when it broke. Next morning the stock opens at 61.50.
questions.q: Short at the open?
choices: No; over 4% under the trigger
Yes; the drop is now confirmed
Yes, at half the usual size
No; never short at the open
questions.answer: No; over 4% under the trigger
questions.why: No. 61.50 is more than 4% under 64.63, and we do not chase a short that far past the trigger. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays over the high, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. Wait for the next setup.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% under the trigger, we do not chase the open. Wait for the next setup.

wrong.Yes; the drop is now confirmed: Confirmed and too far away are both true. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Half of a chased entry is still a chased entry.
wrong.No; never short at the open: Opening under the trigger is still trading through it, so the open is allowed. The 4% line is what blocks this one.

questions.simple: No. The open is already more than 4 percent under the trigger, so a short chases the move and shrinks the size.

deeper.trap: The 4% line is measured from the trigger level, not from where you wish you had filled. Being away from the screen does not open a wider window. A later short needs a new stall and a new close under both averages.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
fixed before (cold check)

questions.story: The app's market filter reads Red, its weakest reading. We hold mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day. A stock under its falling 200-day bounces into its 50-day, makes a lower high, stalls five days and closes under both averages.
questions.q: What is it by our rules?
choices: A candidate; more checks come next
A short now; Red means shorts
A candidate, but Red blocks it
A sell signal for longs, no short
questions.answer: A candidate; more checks come next
questions.why: A short candidate. The filter reads Red, which is mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day. The stock is under a falling 200-day, bounced into the 50-day and made a lower high. That is our own frame: a decent pop back up, rejected at the 50-day or 20-day. In our scan this was the one place the drop separated from the base rate. A candidate is not a trade: the stop, the borrow, the report window and the RS rating still have to pass.
questions.lesson_line: Red market, under the 200-day, a pop that fails at the 50-day: a short candidate. Then run the other checks.

wrong.A sell signal for longs, no short: Above the 200-day it would be. Under a falling 200-day in a Red market it can be the short.
wrong.A short now; Red means shorts: Red and the 200-day are two checks. The stop, the borrow, the report window and the RS rating still have to pass.
wrong.A candidate, but Red blocks it: Red does not block it. Red is mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day, and this stock is under it.

questions.simple: A candidate. Red and a stock under its 200-day allow shorts, but the stop, borrow and report checks come next.

deeper.trap: A candidate is not a trade yet. The stop must be close enough to fit our stop rules. The stock must be easy to borrow. No report may fall in the next 3 sessions, and the RS rating should be 20 or less. Fail one, and it is a skip.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-023, the market filter)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: In August 2011, a bounce dies at the falling 50-day, then a four-day stall. Today it trades down through both averages and the stall low, and closes at 131.23 on 1.2x volume. The day's high is 134.76.
questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first cover day.
choices: Through trigger; stop 134.79; day 3+
Through trigger; stop 134.79; day 1
At the close; stop 134.79; day 3+
Through trigger; stop 133.00; day 3+
questions.answer: Through trigger; stop 134.79; day 3+
questions.why: Short as price trades through the trigger, stop 134.79, first cover on day 3 or later. Shorts enter like buys, never at the close. The stop is a few cents over the day's high of 134.76, the nearest place the idea is wrong. It is about 2.7% from 131.23, inside the 3% we prefer. We very rarely sell on day 1 and usually wait until day 3, selling into strength. Measured from the 131.23 close, GS reached 3R on day 4.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, cover, trail. Write it before it triggers; execute it without a debate.

wrong.Through trigger; stop 134.79; day 1: We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. The first cover is a judgment, usually day 3 or later.
wrong.At the close; stop 134.79; day 3+: Shorts enter like buys, as price trades through the trigger. Never at the close.
wrong.Through trigger; stop 133.00; day 3+: A stop at 133.00 sits inside the day's range, under the high of 134.76.

questions.simple: Short through the trigger, stop a few cents over the day's high where the idea fails, first cover into strength from day 3.

deeper.example: GS, 2011-08-02: the bounce died at the falling 50-day, then a four-day stall, then a close at 131.23. The stop at 134.79 was about 2.7% away. Measured from that close, 3R came on day 4. At best it reached 13.2R, a high-water mark on a fixed stop, not a result to bank.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook and the D-013 first-sell judgment
the short entry on the close is not covered by D-003

questions.story: The chart is an index fund with its name hidden. The trigger day is the last bar, a Friday. The Nasdaq closed under both its averages, the big AI names leading it lower. You hold six longs.
questions.q: What does the index's Wedge Drop tell you?
choices: Get defensive; trim some longs
Buy the dip in the big leaders
Nothing; only single stocks matter
Hold; wait for the 200-day to break
questions.answer: Get defensive; trim some longs
questions.why: Get defensive and trim longs. TraderLion: when an index forms a Wedge Drop, it is a warning that the market as a whole is weakening. Kell: ideally any long positions have been closed at the Wedge Drop. A weak market is a headwind for every long you hold. The job is to cut exposure, not to call the next leg.
questions.lesson_line: When the index wedge drops, your longs are on notice. Reduce first, ask later.

wrong.Buy the dip in the big leaders: Leaders falling through their averages is a sign to get defensive, not to buy.
wrong.Nothing; only single stocks matter: TraderLion names the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. The index's drop is the warning for every long.
wrong.Hold; wait for the 200-day to break: The index's own drop is the warning. The 200-day is a separate gate for shorts.

questions.simple: Get defensive. An index drop warns that the whole market is weakening, and every long you hold feels that.

deeper.trap: Buying the dip treats the drop as a pullback inside a trend. Kell read an index drop as confirmation of a deeper pullback. Waiting for the 200-day treats it as a stock rule. TraderLion reads an index drop as a warning for the whole market.

reasons: a card rule, proposed

questions.story: Kell flags a laggard: a loss of 166.50 would trigger a Wedge Drop short. It closes at 166.35, 19% under its 200-day, in a strong market, and he adds it might just be an avoid.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: Pass; the market is too strong
Short; it is under the 200-day
Short; Kell flagged the stock

questions.q: A stop over the top of a wide stall is acceptable if it sits within about 5% of the entry.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The day's high is the main stop for a short. The pattern's high or a line plus a cushion are acceptable too. We prefer 1 to 3% away and accept up to 5%. The distance matters because the stop sets the size: a wider stop buys fewer shares for the same risk. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. TraderLion's page asks for tight stops on this short.
questions.lesson_line: The stall top is an acceptable stop only inside our stop distance. Past 5%, wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.simple: True. A stop over the stall top is fine if it stays within about 5%, because a wider stop just buys fewer shares.

deeper.counter: A wide stall is not a ban. Wide, loose action grades lower, not out. But the stop is a separate test. A stall top more than 5% away is past what we accept, so we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: A Wedge Drop usually takes months to form, like the classical rising wedge.
questions.answer: False

Our Wedge Drop is different: price rests a few days tight on its moving averages, then falls through them. They share a name, not a time scale, so a search for rising wedge patterns will show you the wrong setup.
questions.lesson_line: Same name, different time scale. Ours is days on the averages, not months of trendlines.
questions.simple: False. The classical rising wedge takes months, while a Wedge Drop is a few quiet days on the averages and then a fall.

A plan; short a break of 166.50 now
A plan; short it first, set a stop
Skip it; a post is no source of ideas

questions.q: You hold what is left of a short and trail the 9 EMA. Price pokes above it at noon, then closes under it. Cover?
choices: No, the close under it keeps you in
Yes, any trade above it is a cover
Yes, cover half and trail the rest
Yes, a poke shows buyers are back
questions.answer: No, the close under it keeps you in
questions.why: No. The trail is the 9 EMA for a fast mover or the 20 EMA for a steadier one. We cover what is left on a close back above it, not on a touch. A poke that fades by the close is noise, and reacting to every poke would shake you out of a working short. Here the stock closed under the line, so the short stays on.
questions.lesson_line: Cover on the close back above the line, not on the poke.

wrong.Yes, any trade above it is a cover: A touch is not a close. We cover only on a close back above the trail, so a poke that fades by the close changes nothing.
wrong.Yes, cover half and trail the rest: What is left comes off in one piece on a close back above the line. A poke that fades by the close changes nothing.
wrong.Yes, a poke shows buyers are back: A poke is not buyers taking over. A rally that stalls under the falling averages is a place to hold.

questions.simple: No. We cover only on a close back above the trail line, because a poke that fades is noise.

questions.q: What do we do now?
questions.story: The chart ends on a quiet day in a six-day rest on the averages. Price has not fallen through them yet.
choices: Wait until it falls through them
Short now; the top is already in
Short now, stop over the stall high
Buy it; a quiet rest means strength
questions.answer: Wait until it falls through them
questions.why: Wait until it falls through them. Kell: the Wedge Drop confirms the reversal when price falls through the moving averages with an influx of sellers. Until then it is only a rest. Shorting inside the rest is early, and one more push up can take the stop. We short as price trades down through the trigger, never before it. The chart is EXP, a six-day rest with the averages flattening.
questions.lesson_line: A rest is only a rest. Short as price falls through the averages, not before.
questions.simple: Wait until it falls through the averages. A rest is only a rest, and the fall is what shows sellers have taken over.

wrong.Short now; the top is already in: A rest is not a drop. Shorting inside the rest is early, and one more push up takes the stop.
wrong.Short now, stop over the stall high: Same mistake with a stop. Until price falls through the averages, buyers have not given up.
wrong.Buy it; a quiet rest means strength: A quiet rest is not strength. Kell: price trades tight into the averages because there are fewer new buyers. We buy on a trigger, not a pause.

questions.q: Does the light volume void the setup?
questions.story: The chart ends on the drop day. The stall was tight, and the drop came on light holiday volume, 0.4 times the usual. Everything else checks out. Our grade is our judgment of how clean a setup is, and it sets the size.
choices: No; heavy volume only adds to the grade
Yes; a drop needs heavy volume to count
Yes; light volume means no sellers came
No; but we halve the size
questions.answer: No; heavy volume only adds to the grade
questions.why: No. Volume raises the grade, but it is not a requirement for the setup to count. Kell calls the drop an influx of sellers, and the fall under both averages and the stall low is what shows it. In our scan, heavy volume raised the win rate but not the average R. GEN dropped on 0.4 times the usual volume in a holiday week and went on to reach 18.0R at best.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume lifts the grade. A drop on light volume still counts.
questions.simple: No. Heavy volume only adds to the grade, so a drop on light volume still counts as a Wedge Drop.

wrong.Yes; a drop needs heavy volume to count: Volume raises the grade. It is not a requirement for the setup to count.
wrong.Yes; light volume means no sellers came: The fall under both averages and the stall low is what shows sellers took over. Volume raises the grade, but it is not a requirement.
wrong.No; but we halve the size: We have no halving rule for light volume. Volume only raises the grade, so a light drop just earns no lift.
